ince of Ontario and the town of Brampton combined their efforts to bring about that diversion. Believe me, some of the Liberals in the legislature were rubbing their hands in glee because it seemed to them the province was spending a large sum of money, without any tangible results. "Hurricane Hazel," however, showed the foresight of the then premier of Ontario, Colonel T. L. Kennedy, because the town of Brampton was saved from that hurricane.
That is the kind of foresight the minister must show if he is going to encourage steps toward national conservation. He must not try to shilly-shally behind the facade of dominion-provincial rights. I believe agriculture in Canada has pretty well overcome that handicap, and I see no reason why other ministers should not follow a similar course.
For the reasons I have indicated, I support the resolution.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is only very occasionally that hon. members have the opportunity to discuss matters of really fundamental importance to the whole population. We spend a great deal of our time discussing relations with each other and a lesser time discussing our relations with people in other national groups, but very seldom do we discuss our relationship with our environment. I think it would be a good idea if sometimes human beings were to forget their exalted role as something just slightly less than the angels, and regard ourselves as an extremely voracious species of animal that is rapidly eating itself out of house and home.
We have built, on the resources of this globe, various social and political institutions, and we have developed various philosophies; but the whole edifice will fall around our ears unless we deal with this question of abuses in our life on this planet. This requires the adoption of policies that will see to it that those resources provide the most fruitful returns for the enrichment of human life.
I am not saying that we have not improved considerably in our outlook in this regard within recent years. I can remember very well 40 years ago on the Pacific coast when each summer we had a haze of smoke all over the lower mainland because of the vast quantity of timber that was being burned, due to human greed and human stupidity. Now that is almost a thing of the past. We have been able to curb some of the more flagrant examples of waste in our various industries in British Columbia.
It was about 11 years ago that I appeared as a witness before the royal commission headed by Mr. Justice Sloan which dealt with

the forest products industry in British Columbia. It was on that occasion that I first heard promulgated the idea of a forest management licence, to which reference has been made this afternoon. There was a very interesting incident at that time which I think throws some light on the problem of the conservation of our natural resources.
I may say that the idea was advanced by the spokesman of one of the largest lumber corporations on the British Columbia coast. When he advanced the idea, commission counsel questioned him very closely about it, and asked whether his company really believed they would have financial resources sufficient to fulfil their side of the bargain, which was to provide a continuing supply of new timber in return for cutting rights on existing stands of mature timber. This was in connection with the proposal of a forest management licence.
I shall always remember what the representative of that large lumber corporation said. His reply was, "Oh, I think so-that is, so long as conditions stay the way they are today. But of course if times get tough we might feel it would pay us better to get a pair of scissors and clip coupons." That gave me an inkling of the sense of public responsibility large lumber corporations in British Columbia have toward the development of our natural resources.
Much has been said about the development of the forest management licence scheme. This was brought about as a result of the deliberations of that royal commission; and the royal commission was established because of conditions which had become evident for many years past. The chief forester in the province was the late E. C. Manning who, some may recall, was killed in the aeroplane crash in which the late Hon. Norman McL. Rogers met his death. Mr. Manning year after year had been warning the provincial legislature in Victoria that time was running out in the forests of British Columbia; that there was serious and dangerous overcutting in all species; that no care was being taken to reforest the logged-off lands, and that our backlog of logged-off and totally barren land was increasing at the rate of some 25,000 to
35,000	acres a year in the coast forest alone.
I should say this, Mr. Speaker, to illustrate the importance of the forest stands not merely for the people of British Columbia, not merely for the people of Canada, but for the people of the whole world. The forests of British Columbia constitute over half the total timber resources of Canada. The coast forests constitute the last remaining stand of virgin soft timber in the world, and as a consequence I say they are the responsibility
Conservation
and concern not just of the people of British Columbia, not even just of the people of Canada, but of the people of the whole world.
The forest management licence idea was based on a very sound principle. It was based on the principle that forest products are a continuing resource, if properly harvested and farmed; but the forest management licence system of British Columbia did not take into account a very important factor in the situation, namely the enormous backlog of logged-off timber lands in the most valuable timber growing areas of Canada. At the present time some million and a half totally barren acres of what was formerly the richest timber land in the world exist on the coast of British Columbia. In the 10 years since forest management licensing was started there has been an ominous silence from the licensees under that act. We get very little in the way of reports of the actual areas that have been reforested by the licensees, very little in the way of reports of the manner in which logging operations are now being conducted. There are, I am aware, some companies, some licensees, that have adopted modern silvicultural methods; there are others which definitely have not.
I say the principles are sound, but they have not taken into account the factor of this enormous backlog that can now be overcome only by a vast capital expenditure. In that connection I should like to refer the house to the view of the late Professor George Drummond of the University of British Columbia, an economist who had specialized in forest economics. Ten years ago he was asked to prepare a brief on forest economics for a royal commission. Professor Drummond had this to say. It was his considered conclusion that it was impossible to expect private enterprise to undertake the task of growing new crops of trees. He said: Except in times of exceptional economic activity, with very high prices and with exceptionally low taxation, no large company could be expected to undertake this enormous economic and financial responsibility.
Still less could they be expected to undertake the job of reforesting areas which had been logged off in past years and are now completely barren. At the time of the royal commission in 1944 and 1945 I pointed this out to the royal commissioners and suggested that here was a field into which the provinces would probably have to step. At that time I suggested also that it might now have already gone beyond the point where it was within the financial scope of the province, that it was in fact a national problem and one in which Canada as a whole should be taking a hand.

Conservation
No one knows at the present time just what the situation is with regard to that enormously important natural resource, the softwood stands on the coast of British Columbia. There are conflicting reports both as to the inventory and as to the volume and age of the immature stands of timber; but I will say this, Mr. Speaker. Past experience has proven beyond a doubt that the time is coming when the public interest will demand a major public capital investment in those stands which will be beyond the resources of the province of British Columbia and I think should be considered beyond their competence.
In fact, sir, I would go so far as to say I think it is a very dubious proposition that a major natural resource of that sort, and major natural resources, for instance, such as the oil of Alberta, the iron ores of Ontario, of Quebec and of Newfoundland should be considered solely the responsibility and solely the property of the people who dwell in the various provinces. They are matters that concern all the people of Canada. We are coming now to the point, Mr. Speaker, where we are beginning to consider the global control of many of these vital natural resources.
I suggest to you, sir, that if Canada is going to play its part in the discussions that must take place with regard to the allocation of the remaining resources in the world, then we must have a unified, integrated national policy. It will not do for our Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to go to an international conference and say, "Well, it is unfortunate, but I must call up the premier of British Columbia and put in a telephone call to the premier of Alberta and another one to the premier of Quebec to see whether we can agree with this proposition that you put up"; because that is the state we will be in if we do not establish some sort of national policy with regard to these resources.
The minister has suggested that the resolution we are debating attempts to cover too much territory, to provide too heavy an agenda for the proposed dominion-provincial conference. I presume that might be true if one considered it a conference that was going to go on for a short time and disband. But my concept of it is that it would be a conference that would at least set up a continuing body to study and co-ordinate policies in this field.
In that regard I would point out the experience of our friends to the south, who after countless and repeated experiments in piecemeal control, this state doing it this way, that state doing it that way, each state
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo) .1
demanding some help from the federal government but not prepared to co-ordinate its policies, set up a national conservation commission in the United States not to determine and dictate policies to the states but to meet with the state representatives to devise a unified, integrated program to which the federal government could contribute. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we have as much capacity as our United States friends to deal with this agenda. Surely we have an equal capacity to meet with our fellow Canadians in every province to evolve some sort of a unified national policy.
I cannot help thinking, Mr. Speaker, that it is political considerations that prevent the government from taking the essential step at this time. I would conclude, sir, by reminding the minister that no doubt constitutionally and legally he is perfectly right, but he is rather like the man in the jingle who was right as he stepped along, but he is just as dead as if he had been wrong.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
When I came into the house this afternoon it was not my intention to speak on this resolution, but I usually come into the house prepared to speak on anything that I happen to feel like speaking on. So many references have been made to what agriculture does and what others might do that I thought I might take a little time to indicate some of the things agriculture does.
Before proceeding to do that I should like to read the resolution again. The resolution says:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of calling a dominion-provincial conference on conservation with a view to the establishment of a national policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada.
In the first place the resolution assumes that there is not a national policy now. I should like to suggest that if there is one on these different matters, then the necessity for calling a conference of this kind is obviously nonexistent.
I can quite understand a member of the house who sits with either of the groups on the other side at the far end having that opinion, but I can scarcely understand my hon. friends immediately opposite having such an opinion. I have not taken the trouble to go back over the history of these matters to find out which party in power from time to time established the different policies which we have, but I do know that we have had policies on all these matters ever since I came into the house.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Could the minister tell me where I can find the last statement on a national policy in connection with forestry?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
The hon. member can find it by understanding what is being done in the different departments over the years. I shall come to that in a minute. He probably will not need to look further after I have finished my speech.
I repeat that ever since I have been in this house one of my chief duties has been to learn just what my hon. friend has asked me to state to him, and then keep right on doing it. Any minister who comes into this house representative of any party would find exactly the same situation in relation to most of the important problems that concern the people of this country. For anyone to suggest that there has never been a national policy in relation to forestry is to misunderstand two things. In the first place, as the minister said a few moments ago, with the exception of three provinces natural resources have since confederation been under the control of the provincial governments. They were under the control of the federal government for a considerable period of time in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and it is only since 1931 that they have been under the control of those provincial governments.
Forests, lands, waters and all other matters associated with natural resources were retained when the prairie provinces were set up, and were therefore handled from Ottawa. But the natural resources of all the other provinces right from the time they came into confederation were under the control of the provincial governments. Those provinces had control of their own resources and they were very much concerned that they should have control of them.
The provinces were responsible for their development, and they carried on that development. To say there has been no national policy is to state what is not a fact. There has always been a national policy in relation to resources. The government of Canada-it does not make any difference whether it was a government elected by the supporters of the party who sit directly opposite or a government made up of members who are seated behind us in this particular session-has always had a national policy. Members who have come here from the different provinces of Canada have always insisted on there being a national policy.
That national policy relates to the matters which were raised this afternoon by one hon. member sitting directly opposite-I think it was the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness)-when he called attention to the
Conservation
fact that winds do not stop at boundary lines, that many rivers do not stop at boundary lines, that erosion whether by wind or water is something that a province cannot control completely. In addition, there are insects which fly over the country and destroy forests. It has always been recognized that there was no way of stopping them at boundaries. Therefore there have been understandings over a long term of years as to how such questions could be dealt with by means of co-operation between the provinces and the federal government.
Reference was made to that fact a few moments ago by the minister, when he said the Department of Agriculture did certain things in connection with these problems, and his department did certain things in relation to them. So we have a policy-I am not going into the details of it-which has been set up for a long period of years, of trying to control insects which destroy forests, trying to control the different diseases that attack trees in order to prevent the destruction of our forests. This work has been carried on with complete co-operation between the provinces and the federal government through a definite national policy established for that purpose.
Just within the last half hour we have had it shown very clearly that in 1953 the minister who was administering the department of resources before the minister who spoke this afternoon brought in a bill which provided the leadership which my hon. friends have been asking for this afternoon, in connection with the control of streams and water within the provinces.
The Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act gave leadership in this way. Ever since I came to this house, and long before I came here-I suppose ever since confederation-Ontario has been coming to the government here and saying they were having difficulties on the Thames river, on the Humber river or on other rivers within this province. We were asked to help in providing controls of some kind or another, either to build dams, to widen the stream or deepen the bed of the river in order to carry away the water.
As was said this afternoon, right down to the time this government came into office there was no definite plan as to how this work could or should be done. It was simply a matter of coming to Ottawa when they had a problem, trying to get whatever money they could in order to deal with the particular problem, and then going home and proceeding with the work.
The Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act which was placed on the statute books in 1953 definitely states that whenever

Conservation
a province has a problem of that kind the federal government will provide up to 37J per cent of the cost. It is presumed that the municipalities concerned will pay 25 per cent, leaving the province and the federal government to divide the remaining 75 per cent of the cost. That is a policy, that is a plan recognizing the fact that the province has a responsibility and will at least control the development which is going to take place in order to bring about the results they desire. They know they can come here and if they put up a reasonable proposition to the government they can get that much assistance in connection with the undertaking.
I repeat that there was no plan here in connection with matters of that kind until this government came into power. Previous governments dealt with the question, piecemeal if you like; they dealt with each problem as the problem arose. For many years there was a prolem down in the maritime provinces which was causing a great deal of trouble. This had to do with the control of water; with the control of the ocean, which is not so easy. Account had to be taken of the fact that down there the tides rise to levels found in very few parts of the world, if any. When those waters rose to their heights they came in over the land.
It is quite proper to say that before there was a federal government in Canada at all there were people who found ways of dealing with that problem. They did not live on this continent. Some of them lived over in France. For one period they took care of it. For another period it was under British control, and the British took care of it. You might say that some of these works were probably done in the aftermath of war in order to give employment to men who otherwise would have been out of employment, just as we are talking about similar undertakings now in this country. Nevertheless, whatever the reason was, they found ways and means of putting in dikes and aboiteaux down along the coast and prevented that water from coming in. Then after those dikes and aboiteaux had served their purpose for probably 100 years; after they wore thin, and the waves of the ocean dug underneath the dikes and they fell into the ocean, somebody started talking about it.
Under the constitution of this country it was a provincial responsibility. Nobody questions that fact. Everyone agrees that it was a provincial responsibility. No government had dealt with it before. I have said here on the floor of the house before, and I am going to say it again now, that it took this government 13 years to convince many people that it was more than a provincial question.

So after 13 years of discussion we now have a system which was set up by the passing of an act in Nova Scotia, the passing of an act in New Brunswick, the passing of an act in Prince Edward Island, and the passing of an act here. Under these pieces of legislation we have expended millions of dollars in carrying out a plan which, when it is completed, will as completely control the ocean coming in over these lands as did the old dikes and aboiteaux that were put there by the French and the British in years gone by. I recite this history in order to say again that this government has not been without plans in these matters.
In a few moments I shall deal with some of the questions that were raised by western members, but before doing that I again want to call attention to the fact that the very first words used in the active part of the resolution are "with a view to the establishment of a national policy on soil". That is the important question in so far as agriculture in this country is concerned, though I must say that in most countries of the world forestry is considered to be a part of agriculture. There is a reason why it has not been so considered in this country. The reason is that we have eleven different governments and the natural resources of this country have been under the provincial governments. Where you have one government, and in some places where you even have a federated form of government, forestry is considered to be a matter of planting and harvesting just like all other agriculture. So trees are planted.
I was never so surprised at anything as I was on the first trip I made up the east side of the Alps. I found that there were more sawmills on the east side of the Alps than there are in Canada. When people started to talk to me about coming out to this country to engage in lumbering I had to say to them, "You must get into your minds an entirely different picture from the one you have here". There is a little sawmill in practically every town and in places that are not towns at all up over the sides of the mountains. I made inquiries as to how they could go on lumbering in that area to the extent they were, and I was told that every time you cut a tree in that section of the continent of Europe, you must plant one. Whoever cuts it is responsible for putting another tree in its place. There is only so much of it that can be cut. It goes on growing over the years. There is a constant supply of timber there to keep their little mills going, and so they have a supply of lumber.
This country has not followed that practice. One of the statements made this afternoon was that up at the source of the Humber

river, or up at the sources of some of the other rivers in Ontario all the timber was cut off and, as a result, in the spring the snow melts more rapidly than it did before, water rushes down in these streams and causes floods and erosion of the soil; and suggestions have been made as to what ought to be done about it. I do not know of any place which is as young as the province of Ontario where I have come across as many places where they are planting trees and doing reforestation, whether it be over in Scotland where they have a great deal of it, or whether it be on the continent of Europe where they have considerable of it.
I must give credit to the province of Ontario. I do not know whether it was started under a Liberal government or a Tory government, but all up through this province, for example as you go from here to Prescott, you see plantings of evergreen trees. Everybody knows to what party Mr. Howard Ferguson belonged. You can see the place from which they get their trees, which is marked "The Howard Ferguson nurseries", just off the side of the road. All through that country you find trees being planted. Down in my own section of Ontario where I was born and raised the sharp corners of the three-cornered sections of land are planted in timber. I have been surprised at the way in which it has grown. It is all very well to say to us that we should have been doing something about it. What I am saying to you is that the provinces in this country are doing something about it.
In so far as the plantations out west are concerned, they have been under the control of this government simply because of what I said at the beginning, namely that down until 1931 we were responsible for natural resources. So it is that we have a forestry farm at Indian Head. We have another forestry farm up at Saskatoon. Trees have been given away for years. I went to Regina in 1904 and they were being given away then. They are still being given away. Any farmer can go to these plantations, get trees, take them home and plant them. Reforestation has been carried on in that way over a considerable period of years. So I repeat that policies have been in existence with regard to reforestation, and policies have been in existence with regard to the fighting of insects and the fighting of parasites. As to those policies there is no disagreement as between
Conservation
the provinces and ourselves. We meet together from time to time and discuss them.
There was no necessity for our meeting all the provinces of Canada when we were considering building dikes and aboiteaux in the maritime provinces. We met the three provinces down there and considered the matter. There was no necessity for meeting all the provinces in Canada when we were dealing with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act out in western Canada. The provinces out there were met.
My friend the hon. member for Calgary North stated this afternoon that the Department of Agriculture does something, and asked why the other minister does not also do something. Fortunately for the other minister, I was not always here. I was premier of Saskatchewan before I came here. Whatever other people might think about it, the first meeting with regard to P.F.R.A. was held in the city of Saskatoon. It was called by myself as premier of Saskatchewan. It was attended by John Bracken, who at one time led the party on the opposition side of the house here; he was there representing Manitoba. It was attended by Mr. Reid, who at that time was premier of Alberta. We discussed this whole question which had developed as a result of the fact that the provinces now had the natural resources and were responsible in connection with them.
We said, they have simply handed over to us a responsibility which all other provinces admittedly always had. They have handed it over to us after having taken from us the earnings from these lands that had been disposed of, the earnings from disposal of the timber resources, and the earnings from the mining rights. They said here, take it, and go ahead and run it in the best way you can. The proposition was first mentioned by the first government of Mr. King. It was finally carried out by the Bennett government, and we had the resources.
We said at this conference that in view of the fact that these lands and the resources of one kind or another had been disposed of, the federal government should do something more about it before turning them over piecemeal to us. So we proposed a plan similar to the one that was inaugurated in 1935 by the government of Mr. Bennett to deal with what we call P.F.R.A. All I wish to say at this moment is that that did not originate in Ottawa. It originated out on the prairies where the problems were, owing to the fact

Conservation
that the resources had been turned over to the provinces. So we said that, having deprived us of the earnings prior to the time they were turned over, the federal government ought to do something more about it.
I came down here to do something about it. That is practically the reason I am here. I have been here for 20 years, and I remember Mr. Bennett sitting right across from me when we were discussing this question in 1936 and 1937. He said to me, "How long do you think it is going to take to do that job?" The act as we found it only provided for five years at $1 million a year. I said that it was going to take at least 20 years. The 20 years will be up next year, and the job is not completed yet. But what I am saying to hon. members at the moment is that it was not the federal government that started these activities. It was the three provincial governments on the prairies. They asked to have the job done.
It has been said by some hon. members that we should be talking about all four western provinces and not three. I would say that maybe we ought to be talking about all of the three before we talk about the fourth. P.F.R.A. does not cover all of the three prairie provinces. About one-sixth of what is under P.F.R.A. is in Manitoba, about two-sixths are in Alberta and the other three-sixths are in Saskatchewan. In all the remainder of those three provinces not under P.F.R.A. the provincial governments are responsible for all drainage, irrigation and water conservation that is done there, in the same way that provincial governments are in other provinces across Canada.
It has been said that we ought to take in British Columbia. Some suggestion has been made that there is no provision in the estimates this year for taking care of any work going on there. I have here on my desk a statement of expenditure on the Lillooet project in British Columbia. The construction and exploration cost was $1,164,000. I arranged that project on one occasion when I was in British Columbia. On the representations made by the people of the area and the province we agreed to spend $100,000 on the project, and it was going to have to be finished by somebody else. Well, it cost us $1,164,000, and it cost somebody else a lot, too.
All I am suggesting is that the federal government has to be careful when it makes arrangements on matters of that kind. There must be plans, yes; there must be policies, yes. There is not a province in Canada that

can have more earnings from its natural resources than British Columbia, and a very small part of those earnings will be from farm lands. There is not another province that has possibilities of greater earnings; and under the constitution the province has always been responsible for the development and reaps the returns. The provinces just over the mountains have not always been responsible, but they are now.
We had said to the former government of the province of British Columbia that we did not think we should go along with this matter much further without some very definite arrangements being made in connection with financing. Then the new government came into office and they asked us the same kind of question. When we said there was no outlined plan upon which we could proceed the statement made to us-and it is in the correspondence which will be tabled here -was to the effect that the government of British Columbia could not afford to do this job, that if they did it in one or two cases they would have to do it over the whole province. I must say that I had to say to them that if we did it in one or two cases we would have to do it over the whole province. So we thought some very definite plans should be made before there was any further expenditure of money on projects of that kind.
What I started out to say was that I have here the figures of the expenditures under a definite plan in connection with this matter. Under that definite plan we have spent $89 million in the four western provinces in order to do the very kind of work that it is presumed should be done under the resolution. Therefore I say to hon. members that we are not opposing the doing of that kind of work. We all agree with everything that has been said in the house this afternoon with regard to the necessity of having it done. We simply say that under our constitution there are ways of doing it properly and there are ways of trying to do it improperly and only getting into difficulties.
Therefore we suggest that if we stay with the constitution as it is and go on and do the job as we have been doing it, eventually it will be done properly. But if we attempt to go off on some tangent and do something else simply because of a resolution being moved in the house we will have great difficulties.

The information is as follows:
Soil survey work in Canada is conducted by the experimental farms service in co-operation with the provinces, roughly on the basis of costs being shared equally. In addition to co-operating in field survey activities the experimental farms service acts as a co-ordinating agency. Headquarters for soil survey work by the experimental farms is with the field husbandry division on the central farm, Ottawa; provincial headquarters are as follows:
Newfoundland, dominion experimental station, St. John's; Prince Edward Island, dominion experimental station, Charlottetown; Nova Scotia, agricultural college, Truro; New Brunswick, university of N.B., Fredericton; Quebec, agricultural college, Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Macdonald college, Que.; Ontario, Ontario agricultural college, Guelph; Manitoba, university of Manitoba, Winnipeg; Saskatchewan, university of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon; Alberta, university of Alberta, Edmonton; British Columbia, university of B.C., Vancouver, provincial department of agriculture, Kelowna.
The basic program for soil surveys in Canada is a systematic reconnaissance survey of all the present and potential agricultural areas. However, special surveys are often conducted in areas where there is immediate need for soils information for specific purposes. The scope of soil surveys in 1953 is indicated by the fact that in addition to the carrying on of the systematic reconnaissance soil surveys in nearly all the provinces, special soil surveys included examination of the soils in the Fort Chimo district of northern Quebec, inspection of lands in various parts of Newfoundland for the royal commission on agriculture and the provincial department of agriculture, mapping and classification of soils in proposed irrigation projects in

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may have permission to revert to motions I should like to move:
That in relation to the adjourned debate on the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply, and on the amendment thereto, moved February 15, the provisions of standing order 28 be suspended for Thursday, February 17, 1955.
He said: The purpose of the motion will be obvious. It is so that we may continue tomorrow the debate we had yesterday on the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. It has been agreed, sir, that we shall try to have a vote tomorrow night not later than nine o'clock, and of course earlier if it meets the wishes of hon. members. This will permit the airing of other grievances

Business of the House when the vote on the amendment is disposed oi, and we would hope we could complete that before ten o'clock or at a slightly later hour if it should prove necessary.
